title: What "Statistically Significant" Means
objective: After this level you can explain honestly what a significant result and a p-value tell you: how surprising the data would be if nothing were going on.
summary: Fisher's tea test shows the idea of significance: how surprising would this be by luck? A p-value measures that; it is not the chance a finding is true.

cards.headline: A lady said she could taste whether the milk went in first.
cards.body: In his 1935 book The Design of Experiments, the statistician Ronald Fisher turned that claim into a famous test. The question it answers: when is a result too good to be luck?

cards.headline: What would luck look like?
cards.body: Fisher's plan: 8 cups, 4 with milk first and 4 with tea first, served in random order. She had to pick out the 4 milk-first cups. There are 70 ways to choose 4 cups from 8, so someone just guessing would get them all right only 1 time in 70, about 1.4%. Sort all 8 correctly, and pure luck becomes a hard story to believe.

cards.headline: That's what a p-value measures
cards.body: A p-value asks the same question of any study: if nothing were going on, how surprising would results at least this striking be? A small p-value means luck alone would rarely produce them. Fisher wrote that it was usual and convenient to draw the line at 5 percent. Results that clear the line are called statistically significant.
cards.callout: Small p-value: this would be rare if nothing were going on.

cards.fact: A p-value is not the chance the finding is true.
cards.context: That's the classic misreading, and the American Statistical Association warned against it in 2016. A p-value doesn't measure the chance the hypothesis is true, or that the data came from luck alone. So p = 0.05 isn't a 5% chance the result is a fluke. It only says how badly the data fit the idea that nothing is going on.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: a p-value starts by assuming nothing is going on, so it can't also be the chance that something is.

cards.headline: Statistically significant
learned: Tea test: guessing wins 1 time in 70
p-value: how surprising if nothing's going on
Not the chance the finding is true

questions.prompt: In Fisher's tea test, pure guessing would sort all 8 cups correctly _____.

options.label: 1 time in 8
options.rationale: There are 70 ways to pick 4 cups of 8, not 8.

options.label: 1 time in 20
options.rationale: With 4 cups of each kind there are 70 possible picks, so it's rarer than that.

options.label: 1 time in 1,000
options.rationale: Much rarer than guessing really is: 70 possible picks means 1 time in 70.

questions.explanation: There are 70 ways to choose 4 cups out of 8, and only one is right: 1 time in 70, about 1.4%.

questions.prompt: What does a small p-value tell you about a study's results?

options.label: The finding is almost certainly true
options.rationale: The ASA warns a p-value isn't the chance the hypothesis is true.

options.label: The effect is large and important
options.rationale: Significance says nothing about size, as the next level shows.

options.label: The study made no mistakes
options.rationale: A p-value can't check a study for errors.

options.label: Results this striking would be rare if nothing were going on

questions.explanation: A p-value asks how surprising the results would be if nothing were going on. Small means luck alone would rarely produce them.

questions.prompt: Fisher's usual line for significance was 5 percent. Written as Level 7's "1 in N", that is:
questions.explanation: To turn a percent into "1 in N", divide 100 by it: 100 ÷ 5 = 20, so 5% is 1 in 20.
